section_summary: The section opens with the conclusion of an article condemning American financiers and manufacturers for supplying Japan with oil, metals, machinery, vehicles, aircraft, and other strategic materials during the war in China. It then documents sharply increased American exports to Japanese-controlled Manchuria and contains extensive correspondence from churches, peace groups, clergy, teachers, and private citizens urging the Roosevelt administration to halt shipments to Japan. State Department replies repeatedly explain that the Neutrality Act could embargo only enumerated arms, would apply equally to China and Japan, and did not authorize restrictions on commodities such as oil and scrap iron; the section closes with an incomplete letter from a missionary formerly in Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Conclusion of article on American economic assistance to Japanese aggression
subfiles.about: The article argues that American finance and industry were sustaining Japan's war in China through investment and exports of strategic materials.
subfiles.summary: The author attacks George Bogen's advocacy of American participation in Japanese-controlled North China and portrays Wall Street as subverting both public opinion and the Roosevelt administration's China policy. Detailed statistics describe Japanese purchases of American oil, iron, steel, machinery, vehicles, aircraft, and other military necessities, concluding that such trade undermined the Open Door and China's territorial integrity.

subfiles.title: Leon L. Loofbourow to Cordell Hull concerning Canal Zone shipments
subfiles.about: Loofbourow asks Hull to stop ships passing the Canal Zone with materials that enable Japan's invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: Writing from Balboa, Loofbourow says Canal Zone residents regularly see munitions, scrap iron, and other materials carried toward Japan. He calls the traffic a source of sorrow and argues that it makes the United States an unofficial partner in China's destruction.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to telegram on coordinated prohibition of shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a telegram reporting Wellington Koo's proposal for British, French, and American action against shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Wellington Koo urged the three governments to prohibit armament and munitions shipments in response to Japan's southward expansion. The entry notes the apparent success of Washington's moral pressure concerning aircraft deliveries.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on Manchurian imports
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes a Mukden despatch showing a wartime surge in American exports to Japanese-controlled Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: American imports into Manchuria rose to ¥41 million in the first four months of 1938, even as private importers were forced to liquidate for lack of permits. The memorandum concludes that most iron, steel, automobiles, and parts were army purchases or were tied to Japanese war industries and that the Japanese army controlled foreign-exchange spending through Manchukuo.

subfiles.title: Langdon covering despatch forwarding “Imports of War Materials from the United States”
subfiles.from: William R. Langdon, American consul at Mukden
subfiles.about: Langdon forwards a copy of his despatch to the embassy at Peiping on American war-material exports to Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The consul encloses despatch no. 272, dated the same day, entitled “Imports of War Materials from the United States.” The covering despatch was transmitted in quintuplicate to the Department of State.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 272, “Imports of War Materials from the United States”
subfiles.about: Langdon assesses American exports to Manchuria as an overlooked component of Japan's war imports.
subfiles.summary: Quoting a Foreign Policy Bulletin article, Langdon argues that estimates of American support for Japan must include exports to Manchuria. Trade controls excluded ordinary American consumer goods while imports of iron and steel, automobiles, and parts soared, showing that the Japanese army directed Manchukuo's foreign spending toward military needs.

subfiles.title: Senator Maloney's secretary forwarding Chase Kimball correspondence
subfiles.from: Secretary to Senator Francis T. Maloney
subfiles.about: Maloney's secretary forwards another communication from peace activist Chase Kimball for State Department consideration.
subfiles.summary: The letter explains that Senator Maloney remains absent and encloses Kimball's latest communication. It identifies Joseph C. Green and Charles W. Yost of the Office of Arms and Munitions Control as Kimball's previous contacts.

subfiles.title: Chase Kimball to Francis T. Maloney
subfiles.to: Francis T. Maloney, attention Miss Flynn
subfiles.about: Kimball forwards his clarification of a New Haven resolution concerning American aid to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Kimball says the State Department misunderstood the Far East resolution passed at the New Haven meeting. He asks that his explanatory letter be brought to Senator Maloney's attention because the resolution was addressed to Congress as well as the President.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Francis T. Maloney
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges Maloney's forwarding letter and supplies its reply to Chase Kimball.
subfiles.summary: The letter acknowledges the correspondence from Maloney's secretary and Kimball's further views on the Far Eastern situation. It encloses a copy of the Department's response to Kimball and returns Kimball's original letter to the senator.

subfiles.title: Chase Kimball to the Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Green or Charles W. Yost
subfiles.about: Kimball clarifies that the Connecticut Peace Conference sought moral pressure on exporters rather than invocation of the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: Kimball argues that most American copper, automobiles, oil, iron, and machinery sent to Japan fell outside the Neutrality Act and that the New Haven resolution requested broader executive and congressional action. He asks whether aircraft companies complied with Hull's appeal and requests monthly license values for arms exports to China and Japan from January 1937 through September 1938.

subfiles.title: Joseph C. Green's reply to Chase Kimball
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, Office of Arms and Munitions Control
subfiles.about: Green answers Kimball's request about moral pressure and arms-export licenses.
subfiles.summary: Green says the Department noted Kimball's views but used advisory pressure only in the exceptional case of aircraft and aeronautical equipment connected with bombing civilian populations. He reports substantial compliance by manufacturers and supplies a monthly table of licensed arms exports to China and Japan, although much of the table is illegible in the OCR.
keywords: Office of Arms and Munitions Control

subfiles.title: Allen T. Treadway forwarding Harry W. Foot's letter
subfiles.about: Treadway forwards a church association's appeal about American policy in the Sino-Japanese conflict.
subfiles.summary: The representative encloses a letter from the Reverend Harry W. Foot, scribe of the Berkshire North Association. He asks to hear Hull's views on the matter.

subfiles.title: Harry W. Foot to Allen T. Treadway
subfiles.about: Foot conveys a church association resolution opposing further exports of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Berkshire North Association unanimously characterized Japan as an aggressor acting contrary to Christian international ideals. Claiming that American supplies sustained the invasion of China, it asked Treadway to work for the curtailment and termination of those exports.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Allen T. Treadway
subfiles.about: The Department explains why the Neutrality Act had not been invoked against China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply states that a presidential finding of war would prohibit enumerated arms shipments to both belligerents, while no law permitted an embargo against Japan alone or against non-arms commodities. It says Roosevelt judged invocation contrary to American interests and reports licensed arms exports since July 1937 of about $14.27 million to China and $10.79 million to Japan.

subfiles.title: Dudley A. White forwarding an Ohio petition
subfiles.about: White forwards a petition from constituents concerning shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The representative says he is transmitting the enclosed petition at the signers' request. He describes it as self-explanatory and does not add a policy recommendation.

subfiles.title: Mrs. F. B. Roscoe letter and Woman's Christian Temperance Union petition
subfiles.from: Mrs. F. B. Roscoe and other Greenwich, Ohio petitioners
subfiles.about: Roscoe and fellow petitioners ask for action against government-permitted exports of war materials.
subfiles.summary: The poorly preserved letter asks White to help a cause associated with limiting American assistance to warfare. An attached petition signed by members of the Greenwich organization protests the government's allowance of shipments to other nations.

subfiles.title: Joseph C. Green's reply to Mrs. F. B. Roscoe
subfiles.about: Green acknowledges the petition and explains the statutory limits on restricting exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The response says a Neutrality Act proclamation would stop enumerated arms shipments to China as well as Japan, while no such proclamation had been issued. It stresses that scrap iron was outside the statutory arms list and cites approximately $14.27 million in licensed exports to China and $10.79 million to Japan.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Dudley A. White
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges White's referral and encloses its answer to Mrs. Roscoe.
subfiles.summary: The letter identifies Roscoe as corresponding secretary of the Greenwich Woman's Christian Temperance Union and notes the petition's concern with war materials for Japan. A copy of the direct Department reply to Roscoe is enclosed for White's information.

subfiles.title: Robert J. Bulkley forwarding Grace Harley's protest
subfiles.about: Bulkley forwards a constituent's protest against American war-material shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The senator sends Grace Harley's letter to Green for a direct response. He requests notification when the Department has answered her.

subfiles.title: Grace Harley to Robert J. Bulkley
subfiles.about: Harley asks her senator to stop shipments of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Youngstown public-school teacher makes a brief appeal for political action. She asks Bulkley to do everything in his power to halt the trade.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull's reply to Robert J. Bulkley
subfiles.about: Hull acknowledges Harley's letter and encloses the Department's direct response and explanatory materials.
subfiles.summary: The letter confirms receipt of Bulkley's referral concerning exports to Japan. It returns Harley's letter and encloses the reply, the arms-traffic pamphlet, and the relevant joint resolution.

subfiles.title: Joseph C. Green's reply to Grace Harley
subfiles.about: Green explains why the government had not imposed an arms embargo on Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green states that a Neutrality Act proclamation would bar enumerated arms exports to both China and Japan and that Roosevelt had decided invocation was not in the broader national interest. He adds that the statute did not reach ordinary commodities and provides totals for licensed arms exports to the two countries.

subfiles.title: Frank W. Michener on war supplies to Japan and Germany
subfiles.about: Michener questions why the administration permits war supplies to reach potential future enemies.
subfiles.summary: The difficult handwritten letter objects to shipments to Japan and Germany and invokes the Neutrality Act. Michener argues that the aggressor states may become American enemies and asks why resources should be sent to them.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Frank W. Michener
subfiles.about: The Department outlines the legal requirements for embargoing arms to belligerents.
subfiles.summary: The reply says the President had made no finding of a state of war involving either Japan or Germany and that any embargo under the Neutrality Act would apply to both parties to a conflict. It defends presidential discretion, notes that non-arms commodities could not be prohibited, and supplies arms-license totals for China and Japan.

subfiles.title: John Warren Day inquiry concerning alleged J. P. Morgan loans to Japan
subfiles.about: Day asks whether reports that J. P. Morgan financed Japanese purchases of American raw materials are true.
subfiles.summary: Day says Helen Topping quoted Muriel Lester as alleging that the New York banking firm had made several loans to Japan. He asks Yost to verify or refute the claim.

subfiles.title: Maxwell M. Hamilton's reply to John Warren Day
subfiles.about: Hamilton responds to the inquiry about alleged American bank loans to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton restates the allegation that Japanese borrowers used Morgan loans to purchase American raw materials. He says the Department is unaware of any Japanese loans obtained in the United States during the period concerned.

subfiles.title: Mrs. E. H. Brunemeier to Franklin D. Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Brunemeier asks Roosevelt to stop exports of scrap iron, oil, and munitions that sustain Japan's army in China.
subfiles.summary: Writing for hundreds of churchwomen, Brunemeier contrasts fundraising to rebuild bombed missions with American sales that enable further destruction. She asks whether neutrality can be enforced and urges a peace policy that stops aid to belligerents.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost's reply to Mrs. E. H. Brunemeier
subfiles.about: Yost explains why existing law did not authorize an embargo on oil and scrap iron sent to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The response states that a Neutrality Act proclamation would embargo enumerated arms to China and Japan alike and that Roosevelt had decided not to invoke it. Yost emphasizes that oil and scrap iron were not statutory implements of war and again supplies licensed-arms totals for both countries.

subfiles.title: Arthur F. Wahlquist to Franklin D. Roosevelt
subfiles.about: A Methodist pastor and World War veteran appeals to Roosevelt about American exports aiding Japan.
subfiles.summary: Although much of the handwriting is illegible, Wahlquist identifies his wartime service and objects to the continuation of shipments connected with Japan's war. He calls on the President to use his authority to stop the trade.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost's reply to Arthur F. Wahlquist
subfiles.about: Yost answers Wahlquist's protest with the Department's explanation of neutrality law and its aircraft policy.
subfiles.summary: Yost says an arms embargo required a presidential proclamation and would apply equally to China and Japan, while scrap iron lay beyond the government's statutory power. He also notes that Hull publicly condemned bombing civilian populations and that aircraft manufacturers and exporters had been directly advised of that position.

subfiles.title: John Nicholson transmitting the Lompoc church resolution
subfiles.about: Nicholson forwards a church-board resolution urging an end to war-sustaining trade with Japan.
subfiles.summary: The official board of the Methodist Episcopal Church of Lompoc unanimously adopted the resolution on October 3. It describes American trade as making the country a partner in Japan's destruction of Chinese lives and property, and Nicholson adds his personal endorsement.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost's reply to John Nicholson
subfiles.about: Yost acknowledges the church resolution and explains the administration's interpretation of the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: The reply thanks Nicholson for sending the resolution and states that an embargo could follow only a presidential finding of war, after which it would cover China as well as Japan. It says non-arms commodities could not be prohibited and reports the licensed values of arms exports to both countries.

subfiles.title: Instruction to acknowledge letters at Mrs. Roosevelt's request
subfiles.about: The note directs staff to acknowledge certain unanswered letters on behalf of Mrs. Roosevelt.
subfiles.summary: The filing note states that the letters have not yet been acknowledged. It instructs the drafter to say that the replies are being made at Mrs. Roosevelt's request.

subfiles.title: Mrs. H. L. Thompson appeal for action to end the war
subfiles.about: Thompson asks for influence to halt war-material shipments and help bring the war to an end.
subfiles.summary: Only part of the handwritten letter is legible, but it seeks government action and advice on how such action might be organized. Thompson says the writers are praying for peace and asks Mrs. Roosevelt to use her influence.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost's reply to Mrs. H. L. Thompson
subfiles.about: At Eleanor Roosevelt's request, Yost explains the administration's legal position on exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that a presidential war proclamation would stop arms exports to both China and Japan and that Roosevelt had decided invocation was not in the country's interest. He adds that the Neutrality Act did not authorize restrictions on non-arms commodities and provides arms-license totals.

subfiles.title: Lewis E. Leonard to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Leonard reports a Newport church resolution opposing all American sales of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: St. Paul's Methodist Episcopal Church adopted its position at the quarterly conference of October 13. Leonard asks Hull to do everything possible to eliminate what the congregation regarded as an unchristian practice.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost's reply to Lewis E. Leonard
subfiles.about: Yost acknowledges the church's protest and explains the limits of the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: The reply says a proclamation would embargo arms to China and Japan alike and that Roosevelt judged such action contrary to broader American interests. It distinguishes enumerated arms from other commodities and cites the Department's licensed-export totals.

subfiles.title: Metropolitan New York ministers' resolution to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: Congregational and Christian Ministers' Association of the Metropolitan Area of New York
subfiles.about: The ministers petition Hull to use every practicable means to end American trade sustaining Japan's invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: The resolution condemns Japanese aggression, civilian bombing, treaty violations, and the use of American aircraft, shells, oil, scrap iron, and trucks in the war. It asks the Secretary of State to end the traffic and supports workers and commercial groups that refuse to participate in shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Metropolitan New York ministers' resolution to Franklin D. Roosevelt
subfiles.from: Congregational and Christian Ministers' Association of the Metropolitan Area of New York
subfiles.about: A parallel resolution asks the President and Congress to end American shipments supporting Japan's war.
subfiles.summary: The association indicts Japan for violating the Nine-Power Treaty and Kellogg Pact and condemns attacks on Chinese civilians and foreign institutions. It calls for direct or indirect action against the trade and expresses moral support for groups refusing to sell or ship war supplies.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost's reply to Walter A. R. McPherson
subfiles.about: Yost jointly acknowledges the ministers' letters to Roosevelt and Hull and states the Department's policy.
subfiles.summary: The response thanks the association for its resolution but says an arms embargo would require a presidential finding of war and would cover China and Japan equally, while non-arms trade remained beyond the Neutrality Act. Yost adds that the government condemned civilian bombing and had communicated that position directly to American aircraft manufacturers and exporters.

subfiles.title: Incomplete letter from a former Shanghai missionary concerning aid to Japan and American property claims
subfiles.about: The writer urges the United States to withdraw economic support from Japan and press claims for American property destroyed in China.
subfiles.summary: The writer says American aid to Japan betrays democratic ideals and helps destroy China's attempt to build a democratic state. Drawing on missionary experience in Shanghai, the letter alleges deliberate Japanese destruction and use of American property despite promises of protection; the document continues beyond page 662.
